headline: Manasquan Rocks at First Light: Blues to 9 Pounds, Bass Still Ghosting the Bunker
subhead: The jetty crowd is feeding on bluefish while everyone waits for the bunker schools to tip over into the first real striper blitz.
body_markdown:
There were nine guys on the Manasquan Inlet south jetty an hour before sunrise Tuesday, and by the time the sky went from black to gray, at least six of them had a bluefish thrashing at their feet. Ava 27s with green tubes, a couple of white bucktails, one guy working a Yo-Zuri popper like he was still mad at it — didn't matter much what was tied on, the blues were stacked on the last of the outgoing and they weren't picky. That's been the story on this stretch for two weeks now, and it's not changing this week either.

Here's the read: bunker are thick from Sea Bright down through Belmar, pushed tight against the beach and piling into the inlets on the tide changes, and bluefish have been all over them — slashing, cutting bait in half, the whole show. Stripers are a different matter. They're in the neighborhood, no question, showing as marks under the bigger bunker pods and occasionally peeling one off at night, but the water's still sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range that keeps big bass lazy and non-committal instead of aggressive. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the blues and the fluke would carry the load while cooler nights held the real striper trigger back — and that's precisely how it's played out. Nothing wrong with that call holding up, but it also means patience is still the name of the game for anyone chasing linesides.

The moon is building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the piece that matters most right now. Bigger tides mean more water moving through Shark River and Manasquan inlets, which tightens up those loose bunker schools and usually forces the issue. Once you get a night or two of genuinely cooler air behind a front, that's when this thing tips — Raritan Bay and the LI south shore are flagged as the most likely first triggers for a real fall blitz, and this stretch from Sea Bright to Manasquan sits right in the pipeline for that same bait to slide south. It's a matter of when, not if, but nobody should be planning a Saturday around a blitz that hasn't shown up yet.

Bluefish remain the sure thing. Sea Bright rocks have been holding fish on the first two hours of the incoming, with the jetty regulars doing well on bunker spoons and 3-ounce Ava jigs bounced through the wash. Asbury Park's jetties have given up blues in the 4-to-6-pound range on chunked bunker fished on a fish-finder rig in the trough, best in that gray hour before full light. Spring Lake's rock piles have been more hit-or-miss — good one morning, dead the next — which tracks with how scattered these bunker pods still are along the beach. Belmar's been steady on poppers worked over visible bait during the last two hours of the ebb; when the pogies bunch up tight against the jetty rocks, that's your window, and it usually closes fast once the tide slacks.

Fluke fishing is winding down the way it always does this time of year, and there's no sugarcoating that. The back-bay and inlet fish have mostly cleared out for deeper ocean structure ahead of the fall push south. Shark River Inlet is still giving up keeper-class fish on the last of the outgoing, working 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets along the channel edges in 15 to 20 feet, but the numbers are down noticeably from three weeks ago. Manasquan Inlet's channel has produced a few decent fish drifting the deeper water off the Coast Guard station on the incoming, but this is closing-window fishing now, not a bite to build a trip around.

Blackfish season doesn't open here until October, so that's still a few weeks off, and porgies have been a quiet, reliable snack fishery off the Belmar and Manasquan Inlet jetties on bloodworms and clam for anyone bored between blitzes — nothing to write home about, but good for a bucket if the kids are along. No albie signs yet in this stretch; that push is still working its way west from the Rhode Island side and hasn't shown teeth down here.

Looking at the next several days, expect more of the same pattern that's held all week — bluefish active on the tide changes at the usual jetty spots, fluke thinning out but still catchable if you hit the right channel structure, and stripers staying non-committal until the water temperature drops a real notch. If there's only one window worth planning around, it's dawn on the building tide around the full moon — the extra water movement should concentrate bait harder against the rocks at Sea Bright and Manasquan, and that's exactly the kind of setup that's tipped bass into feeding mode in past Septembers when the bunker get squeezed into a tight current seam. Keep an eye on the overnight temperatures over the next week; the first real cool front is the trigger everyone up and down this beach is waiting on, and when it comes through, the jetty country from Sea Bright to Manasquan is as good a bet as anywhere on the coast for the first real blitz of the fall.
